name: Hawassa and Lake Hawassa
summary: Hawassa is the lakeside capital of the Sidama Region, about 273 km south of Addis Ababa, known for its early-morning fish market, hippo boat trips and relaxed lakeshore.
details:
Hawassa sits on the shore of Lake Hawassa in the Rift Valley at about 1,708 m above sea level. It is the capital of the Sidama Region and is home to Hawassa University, one of Ethiopia's major universities. Fishing is an important local industry.

The fish market on the southwest edge of town is the best-known sight. Fishermen bring in their catch from the lake, and marabou storks and other birds gather around the boats. A small park sits right beside the market.

Boat trips on the lake are offered to see groups of hippos. Some visitors cycle the roughly 55 km loop around the lake through shoreline villages.

Tabor hill (originally called Dume hill) rises behind the town and gives views over the city and lake. Amora Gedel is a lakeside park near the southern end of town, close to Lewi Resort and several hotels.
highlights: Lakeside promenade bars at sunset on Piazza Road
bestTimeToVisit: The drier months (roughly October to March) are most comfortable; visit the fish market early in the morning when boats come in.
gettingThere: About 273 km south of Addis Ababa by road via Bishoftu; the Addis Ababa–Hawassa expressway makes the drive quicker. Long-distance coaches (such as Selam and Sky Bus) run from Meskel Square in Addis, taking around 5 to 6 hours. Hawassa also has an airport (Awasa Airport, IATA: AWA) with domestic flights.
tips: Go to the fish market early in the morning; a small entry fee and optional guides have been reported
Agree boat prices before setting off and share the boat to cut the cost
Do not leave food or sugar unattended at lakeside resorts — monkeys may take it
Several hotels in town are called Lewi's; make sure you book the one you mean

name: Lake Langano
summary: A brown-watered Rift Valley lake about 200 km south of Addis Ababa, popular for weekend resorts and described as free of bilharzia, so it is used for swimming.
details:
Lake Langano lies in the Rift Valley at about 1,585 m. It is roughly 18 km long and 16 km wide, with a surface area of about 230 square kilometres and a maximum depth of 46 m.

Its brown colour comes from its mineral content, including high sulphur levels, and does not mean the water is dirty. Unlike most other freshwater lakes in Ethiopia, it is reported to be free of schistosomiasis (bilharzia), which makes it a popular place to swim.

A number of resorts line the shore, and the lake is a common weekend escape from Addis Ababa. It sits right next to Abijatta-Shalla National Park, and the park's main entrance at Horakelo is on the stream between Langano and Lake Abijatta, so the two are easily combined.
highlights: Easy base for Abijatta-Shalla National Park
bestTimeToVisit: October to February is dry and coincides with the best flamingo viewing in neighbouring Abijatta-Shalla; weekends and holidays get busy with visitors from Addis Ababa.
gettingThere: About 200 km south of Addis Ababa by road along the Addis–Hawassa route (roughly 3 to 4 hours, depending on road and traffic).
tips: Book resorts ahead for weekends and Ethiopian holidays
Bring sun protection; there is little shade on the beaches
Combine with a morning visit to Abijatta-Shalla National Park

name: Abijatta-Shalla National Park
summary: A Rift Valley national park protecting two alkaline lakes, Abijatta and Shalla, known for flamingos, great white pelicans and hot springs.
details:
Abijatta-Shalla National Park was established in 1974 and covers about 887 square kilometres, roughly 200 km south of Addis Ababa. Its two alkaline lakes, Abijatta and Shalla, are separated by about 3 km of hilly land, with Mount Fike, the park's highest point, between them. A small saline lake, Chitu, lies south of Shalla.

More than 300 bird species have been recorded. Greater and lesser flamingos gather on Abijatta, Chitu and Shalla, and great white pelicans nest on Shalla. Hot springs bubble up at the northeast corner of Abijatta and along Shalla's shores.

Large mammals such as lions, giraffes and buffalo have disappeared from the area, and few wild animals are easy to see today. Charcoal burning, grazing, settlement and salt extraction have damaged the acacia woodland, so the park is mainly a birding and scenery destination.
highlights: Great white pelicans on Lake Shalla
Views from the hills between the two lakes
bestTimeToVisit: October to February, when large flocks of flamingos usually gather on Lake Abijatta.
gettingThere: About 200 km south of Addis Ababa, east of the Batu (Ziway)–Shashamane highway; roughly 3 to 4 hours by car. The main entrance is at Horakelo, on the stream between Lakes Langano and Abijatta. A 4x4 is recommended for park tracks.
tips: Pay entrance fees at the main gate at Horakelo — tickets may not be sold at other access points
Fees reported online vary; confirm with park staff
There is no accommodation inside the park; stay at Lake Langano
Bring binoculars for birdwatching
confidenceNotes: Entrance fees conflict between sources and were left out. Flamingo numbers vary with lake levels. Security: the park is in East Shewa/West Arsi; UK FCDO advises against all but essential travel to East Shewa zone except the Addis–Hawassa expressway, and the US State Department advisory reportedly lists East Shewa and West Arsi zones as Do Not Travel. Check current advice.

name: Lake Ziway and Tulu Gudo Island
summary: A shallow freshwater Rift Valley lake with hippos, rich birdlife and five islands, including Tulu Gudo with its monastery said by tradition to have sheltered the Ark of the Covenant.
details:
Lake Ziway (also called Lake Batu) is a freshwater lake in the northern Rift Valley, up to 31 km long and 20 km wide, with a surface area of about 440 square kilometres. It is shallow, with a maximum depth of around 9 m. The town of Batu (Ziway) lies on its western shore.

The lake is known for its large bird population and for hippos. Boat trips from the shore pass hippo groups and waterbirds.

The lake has five islands: Debre Sina, Galila, Funduro, Tsedecha and Tulu Gudo. Tulu Gudo, the largest, holds the Maryam Tsion monastery. Local tradition says the Ark of the Covenant was kept there for a time around the ninth century. The islands can only be reached by boat.
highlights: Boat trip to Tulu Gudo island and its monastery
Easy stop on the road between Addis Ababa and Hawassa
bestTimeToVisit: October to January has little rain and is the most popular period.
gettingThere: Batu (Ziway) lies on the main road south from Addis Ababa towards Hawassa, roughly 160 km from the capital (approximate). Islands are reached only by hired boat; the boat ride to Tulu Gudo is reported to take about an hour each way.
tips: Allow a half day for a Tulu Gudo boat trip
Dress modestly at the monastery; women may face restrictions at some Ethiopian monasteries, so ask locally
Agree the boat price and return time before leaving shore

hotels.name: Haile Resort Ziway
hotels.description: Lakeside 3.5-star resort with outdoor pool, children's pool, spa and restaurant according to booking listings.

name: Bishoftu (Debre Zeyit) Crater Lakes
summary: A town about 48 km southeast of Addis Ababa ringed by volcanic crater lakes, popular for lakeside resorts, birdwatching and weekend breaks.
details:
Bishoftu, also known as Debre Zeyit, lies about 48 km southeast of Addis Ababa along the Adama road, at around 1,920 m. It is the main base of the Ethiopian Air Force, and construction of a new Bishoftu International Airport began in January 2026.

The town is surrounded by crater lakes, including Lake Bishoftu, Lake Hora, Lake Bishoftu Guda, Lake Koriftu and the seasonal Lake Cheleklaka. Lake Babogaya is another crater lake popular with visitors. Lake Hora is used for watersports and is the site of the annual Irreechaa thanksgiving festival of the Oromo people.

Several resorts sit on the crater rims, making Bishoftu a common weekend escape from the capital. The town is also the usual stop on day trips to Mount Zuqualla to the south.
highlights: Lake Hora and the Irreechaa festival
Easy day trip from Addis Ababa
bestTimeToVisit: Year-round; the dry season from October to May is most pleasant. Irreechaa is held at Lake Hora around late September or early October, when the town is very crowded.
gettingThere: About 48 km southeast of Addis Ababa via the Addis Ababa–Adama expressway or the older Route 4; under an hour by car in light traffic. Minibuses run frequently from Addis.
tips: Book resorts early for weekends
During Irreechaa, expect very large crowds and road closures
Combine with Mount Zuqualla for a full day out

name: Mount Zuqualla and Monastery
summary: An extinct volcano 3,010 m high, about 30 km south of Bishoftu, with a crater lake and a monastery associated with the saint Gebre Menfes Kidus.
details:
Mount Zuqualla is an extinct volcano that rises to about 3,010 m from the plain roughly 30 km south of Bishoftu. Its summit crater holds Lake Dembel, an elliptical lake about 1 km across. A trail of about 6 km circles the crater rim.

The mountain and lake are sacred to Ethiopian Orthodox Christians and to local Oromo people. Tradition says the monastery was founded by Gebre Menfes Kidus. It was destroyed in 1531 during the campaigns of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim. Two churches were later built: one dedicated to Gebre Menfes Kidus (1880, under Menelik II) and one to Kidane Mihret (from Haile Selassie's reign).

The monastery holds a twice-yearly festival that draws pilgrims. For visitors, the climb is a popular day hike from Addis Ababa, usually combined with the Bishoftu crater lakes.
highlights: Gebre Menfes Kidus monastery and pilgrim festivals
bestTimeToVisit: The dry season (roughly October to May) gives clearer views and easier trails.
gettingThere: About 30 km south of Bishoftu, which is about 48 km from Addis Ababa. Tour listings describe a hike of around 4 hours with about 900 m of climbing; tracks also allow vehicles part of the way.
tips: You need reasonable fitness for the climb
Dress modestly at the monastery and follow local rules
Bring water, warm layers and rain protection — it is cool at 3,000 m
Most visitors go with a guide or on an organised day trip from Addis
confidenceNotes: Hike time and elevation gain come from tour listings. Stay overnight in Bishoftu (see Bishoftu entry). Security: the mountain is in East Shewa zone, outside the 10 km Addis–Bishoftu strip, so UK FCDO advises against all but essential travel there; the US State Department advisory reportedly lists East Shewa as Do Not Travel. Check current advice before going.

name: Debre Libanos Monastery and the Portuguese Bridge
summary: One of Ethiopia's most important monasteries, founded in 1284 by Saint Tekle Haymanot on a terrace above a Blue Nile tributary gorge, with a nearby old stone bridge and gelada baboons.
details:
Debre Libanos monastery lies northwest of Addis Ababa in North Shewa Zone. Saint Tekle Haymanot founded it in 1284 as Debre Atsbo, and it was renamed in the 15th century. Its abbot, the Ichege, was traditionally the second most powerful official in the Ethiopian Church after the Abuna.

The monastery was burned in 1531 and not fully rebuilt until after 1699. None of the original buildings survive. Today the main church, built on Haile Selassie's order in 1961, stands over Tekle Haymanot's tomb and has mosaics and stained glass. An older Church of the Cross is said to hold a fragment of the True Cross, and a nearby cave with a holy spring draws pilgrims.

In May 1937, after an attempt on the life of Italian viceroy Graziani, Italian forces massacred hundreds of monks and many civilians here, one of the worst atrocities of the occupation.

Nearby, a short trail from the Ethio-German Park Hotel leads to a small stone-arch bridge known as the Portuguese Bridge, over the Jemma River gorge. Despite its name, it was probably built by Ethiopians in the late 19th century. Gelada baboons and many birds can sometimes be seen on the gorge edges.
highlights: Debre Libanos monastery and Tekle Haymanot's tomb church
Views into the Jemma and Blue Nile gorge system
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (October to May). Religious festivals bring crowds of pilgrims.
gettingThere: North of Addis Ababa off the main road towards Fiche and Bahir Dar; usually visited as a day trip from Addis (roughly 100 km, approximate).
tips: Dress modestly and remove shoes in churches
Entrance fees are charged at the monastery and the bridge
Spotting geladas depends on luck
Check security advice carefully before going — see notes

name: Menagesha Suba Forest
summary: Thought to be Ethiopia's oldest protected state forest, a highland juniper and podocarpus forest southwest of Addis Ababa that is popular for day hikes.
details:
Menagesha Suba Forest covers about 35 square kilometres on the slopes southwest of Addis Ababa, in the West Shewa Zone of Oromia. The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, describes it as thought to be the oldest preserved state forest in Ethiopia.

Tradition says the original juniper forest had been heavily cut by the 15th century, when Emperor Zara Yaqob ordered it replanted. It has been protected in some form ever since. Tourism material often calls it one of Africa's oldest conservation areas, though this is hard to verify.

The forest is a recognised Important Bird Area and Key Biodiversity Area. Visitors come for walks among tall juniper and podocarpus trees, cool highland air and birdwatching, usually on a day trip from Addis Ababa.
highlights: Walks in old-growth juniper and podocarpus forest
Cool, quiet escape from Addis Ababa
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (October to May); trails are muddy in the main rains (June to September).
gettingThere: Southwest of Addis Ababa, usually reached on a day trip by car or with a tour operator; exact road distance not confirmed.
tips: Bring warm layers — it is cool and can be misty
Go with a guide or tour operator, as signage may be limited
Carry food and water; facilities are basic
confidenceNotes: Thin entry: facts come from search summaries of the Kew factsheet and tourism pages; the Kew and BirdLife pages could not be fully read. Coordinates, distance, entry fees and visitor facilities not confirmed. Security: the forest is in West Shewa zone. UK FCDO advises against all but essential travel on the A4 road between Addis Ababa and Cheliya and against all travel north of the A4 in West Shewa; whether the forest access road falls in these areas was not confirmed. The US advisory reportedly lists West Shewa as Do Not Travel. Check current advice.

name: Adadi Mariam Rock-Hewn Church
summary: A monolithic rock-hewn church about 66 km southwest of Addis Ababa, traditionally attributed to King Lalibela and the closest such church to the capital.
details:
Adadi Mariam is a rock-hewn church of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, about 66 km southwest of Addis Ababa. It is thought to date from the late 12th or early 13th century.

Local tradition credits the Zagwe king Lalibela, builder of the famous churches at Lalibela, with commissioning it. Like those churches, it was carved down into the rock rather than built up.

It is often combined with the nearby prehistoric site of Melka Kunture and the Tiya stelae on a day trip south of Addis Ababa. The Hill Museum and Manuscript Library has recorded manuscripts held at the church.
highlights: Easy combination with Melka Kunture and Tiya
gettingThere: About 60–67 km south-southwest of Addis Ababa by road (sources differ); usually visited on a day trip by car.
tips: Dress modestly and remove shoes before entering
A priest or caretaker usually opens the church; a small fee or donation is common
Combine with Melka Kunture on the same day
confidenceNotes: Wikipedia is inconsistent on the zone (it lists North Shewa but the site is in the Southwest Shewa area south of Addis); dating is approximate. The fee/caretaker tip is general practice, not confirmed for this church. Security: UK FCDO does not list this area by name; the US State Department advisory reportedly lists several Shewa zones as Do Not Travel. Check current advice.

name: Melka Kunture and Balchit Prehistoric Sites
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage prehistoric site on the upper Awash River about 50 km south of Addis Ababa, with stone tools and human fossils spanning about 1.7 million years.
details:
Melka Kunture lies on the upper Awash River, across from the village of Melka Awash, about 50 km south of Addis Ababa. It was discovered in 1963, and more than 30 prehistoric occupation sites have been found there.

The finds cover the Oldowan, Acheulean, Middle Stone Age and later Stone Age, with Oldowan remains about 1.7 million years old. Fossils include Homo erectus, Homo heidelbergensis and early Homo sapiens. The nearby Balchit obsidian outcrops, about 7 km away, supplied stone for tools from the earliest times.

In 2024 UNESCO inscribed the site as "Melka Kunture and Balchit: Archaeological and Palaeontological Sites in the Highland Area of Ethiopia". An on-site museum with exhibit buildings and an open-air area shows excavated sites and finds, and three waterfalls lie on the Awash downstream of the bridge.
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (October to May), when tracks to excavation areas are easier.
gettingThere: About 50 km south of Addis Ababa by road; often combined with Adadi Mariam and the Tiya stelae on a day trip.
tips: A local guide helps explain the excavation areas
Combine with Adadi Mariam church nearby
Bring sun protection and water
confidenceNotes: Museum status is from Wikipedia (a new World Bank-funded museum was under construction in 2016); current opening hours and fees not confirmed. Security: the area south of Addis is not named in UK FCDO zone warnings; the US State Department advisory reportedly lists several Shewa zones as Do Not Travel. Check current advice.

name: Dorze and Chencha (Gamo Highlands)
summary: Highland villages above Arba Minch where the Dorze people build tall beehive-shaped bamboo houses and weave colourful cotton cloth.
details:
The Dorze are a Gamo community living in the Gamo Highlands of southern Ethiopia, mostly in villages near Chencha and Arba Minch. The area lies high above the Rift Valley, at elevations above 2,500 m near Chencha.

The Dorze are famous for their tall huts built from hardwood poles and woven bamboo with thatch roofs. Reported heights range from about 8 to 12 m, and the houses can last for decades — up to around 80 years. Because the frame is made of poles, a house can even be moved.

Weaving is a main livelihood, and Dorze textiles are known for their bright colours. Enset (false banana) is a staple food, and its fibres are also used for ropes and mats. Visits usually include a house interior, the weaving cooperative where women spin and men work the looms, and enset bread preparation.
highlights: Mountain views over the Rift Valley lakes
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (October to March); rains, especially April–May, can make the steep road difficult.
gettingThere: Dorze village is about an hour's drive (roughly 28–35 km, sources differ) up a steep road from Arba Minch towards Chencha. Arba Minch has domestic flights from Addis Ababa.
tips: A local guide is normally required in Dorze villages
Ask before photographing people
Bring warm clothes — it is much cooler than Arba Minch
Overnight options are few; book ahead

name: Senkelle Swayne's Hartebeest Sanctuary
summary: A small grassland sanctuary west of Shashamane created to protect the endangered Swayne's hartebeest, which is found only in Ethiopia.
details:
Senkelle Swayne's Hartebeest Sanctuary was established in 1972 and covers about 54 square kilometres. It lies about 10 km south of the Shashamane–Arba Minch road near the town of Aje, and Hawassa is the nearest city.

Its main purpose is to protect the Swayne's hartebeest, an endangered antelope. The herd once numbered about 3,000 but has fallen sharply because of poaching; recent estimates range from a few hundred to about 500 animals.

Other mammals include Bohor reedbuck, warthog, greater kudu and oribi, along with crested porcupine, aardvark and Abyssinian hare. Over the past 30 years, bushland has spread into the grassland, which reduces the hartebeest's habitat.
highlights: Endangered Swayne's hartebeest at close range
Open grassland game walks or drives
Short trip from Hawassa or Shashamane
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (October to March), when tracks are passable and animals are easier to spot in the open grassland.
gettingThere: About 10 km off the Shashamane–Arba Minch road near Aje; Hawassa is the nearest city with an airport and hotels.
tips: Stay in Hawassa and visit on a half-day trip
A 4x4 or local guide helps on the access track
Bring binoculars
confidenceNotes: Thin entry based mainly on Wikipedia; current fees, ranger services and animal numbers not confirmed. The sanctuary is in West Arsi zone. UK FCDO gives no specific warning for West Arsi, but the US State Department advisory reportedly lists East and West Arsi as Do Not Travel. Check current advice.

name: Yabelo, Borana Singing Wells and El Sod Crater
summary: Yabelo is the main town of Borana country in far southern Ethiopia, a base for the Borana 'singing wells', the El Sod salt crater and endemic birds such as Stresemann's bushcrow.
details:
Yabelo is the administrative centre of Borena Zone, at about 1,857 m, northwest of Moyale near the Kenyan border. The Borana, an Oromo pastoralist people who move long distances with cattle and camels, are the main group in the area. The town's Saturday market is a good time to visit.

In this semi-arid land, the Borana have dug wells up to about 30 m deep. Men and women form a human chain inside the well, passing buckets of water up by hand while singing to keep the rhythm, as cattle wait to drink.

El Sod (Chew Bet, meaning 'salt house' in Amharic) is a saline crater lake where the Borana harvest salt that is traded as far as northern Kenya. Visitors reach it by a short but steep hike along the donkey path used to carry salt out.

The Yabelo Wildlife Sanctuary and the larger Borena National Park protect Swayne's hartebeest, Grévy's and plains zebra, gerenuk and Guenther's dik-dik. Birders come for Stresemann's bushcrow and the white-tailed swallow, both found only in this area.
highlights: El Sod salt crater lake hike
bestTimeToVisit: Dry seasons (roughly December to March and July to September) are best for wells, when herds come to water; rains can make tracks difficult.
gettingThere: Yabelo lies on the main Addis Ababa–Moyale road far south of Hawassa; most visitors arrive by 4x4 with a tour operator. Distances were not confirmed in sources.
tips: Visit the wells with a local guide and ask permission before photographing
The El Sod hike is steep and hot — go early and carry water
Fuel and services are limited; plan ahead
confidenceNotes: No hotels in Yabelo could be confirmed. Best-season advice is approximate. Dublock (Dubuluk) wells were not confirmed in sources. Security: UK FCDO advises against all travel within 10 km of the Kenya border (except principal roads and towns) and against all but essential travel to Guji, West Guji and East Borena zones (the Hawassa–Mega road is excepted). The US State Department advisory reportedly lists Borena and Guji as Do Not Travel. Check current advice carefully.

name: Wondo Genet Hot Springs
summary: A forested hillside town southeast of Shashamane known for its natural hot springs and a historic resort hotel that was once a royal retreat.
details:
Wondo Genet is a town in the Sidama Region, southeast of Shashamane and near Hawassa, at about 1,723 m. It is known for its hot springs and lush forest, and is home to a College of Forestry founded in 1977 with Swedish help.

The Wondo Genet resort hotel opened in 1964 on land that was a royal family recreation site until 1975. It is now run by the state-owned Wabe Shebelle Hotels Enterprise and has about 40 rooms, a restaurant, a bar and swimming pools fed by the hot springs.

The forest around the springs is popular for walks and birdwatching. Lonely Planet notes that the concrete pools are functional rather than luxurious.
bestTimeToVisit: Year-round; the dry season (October to March) is best for forest walks.
gettingThere: Southeast of Shashamane and a short drive from Hawassa (distance not confirmed).
tips: Bring a swimsuit and sandals for the pools
Facilities are basic — manage expectations
Visit on a half-day trip from Hawassa

hotels.name: Wondo Genet Resort Hotel (Wabe Shebelle)
hotels.description: State-run hotel opened in 1964 with about 40 rooms, restaurant, bar and hot spring pools.

confidenceNotes: Hotel details come from a 2014 blog and search snippets; current condition and room count may have changed (reviews are mixed). Security: UK FCDO has no zone-level warning for Sidama; search snippets of the US advisory list Sidama among Level 3 areas. Check current advice.

name: Gedeo Cultural Landscape
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape (2023) of layered coffee-and-enset agroforestry, sacred forests and thousands of ancient stelae around Dilla in Gedeo Zone.
details:
The Gedeo Cultural Landscape lies in the highlands along the Rift Valley in Gedeo Zone, whose main town is Dilla. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage cultural landscape in 2023 under criteria (iii) and (v).

The Gedeo people farm in layers: enset (false banana) grows alongside coffee and shrubs under a canopy of tall trees. Patches of natural forest are kept as sacred places where no trees are cut. This system, guided by traditional institutions such as the Songo council of elders and the Ballee system, produces high-quality organic coffee, including the famous Yirgacheffe coffee traded through Dilla.

The slopes are also dotted with dense clusters of megalithic stelae used in Gedeo rituals, thought to date from roughly the 8th to 15th centuries. The main stelae groups are Tuto Fela (about 320 stelae), Chelba-Tutiti (about 1,530) and Sede-Merkato (about 663). Some were used for burials, but their full purpose is still unclear.
highlights: Tuto Fela and Chelba-Tutiti stelae fields
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (roughly October to March); coffee harvest is usually in the later part of the year.
gettingThere: Dilla lies on the main Addis Ababa–Moyale road south of Hawassa. Visiting all the stelae sites takes about a full day; a 4x4 is recommended for side tracks.
tips: Base yourself in Dilla
Hire a local guide to find the stelae sites
Combine with a coffee farm visit around Yirgacheffe

hotels.name: Delight Hotel

name: Jimma and the Palace of Abba Jifar
summary: Jimma is the main city of southwest Ethiopia's coffee country, and nearby Jiren holds the wooden palace of King Abba Jifar II, ruler of the Kingdom of Jimma.
details:
Jimma is a large city in southwest Oromia at about 1,780 m. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Jimma and is a centre of coffee country. The national Jimma Research Center, founded in 1968, works on coffee and spice improvement.

The Palace of Abba Jifar stands at Jiren on a hill just outside the city centre. It was built in the late 19th century by King Abba Jifar II. The World Monuments Fund calls it the most important heritage site in Oromia. It is a timber building with carved wooden balconies, symmetrical staircases and a courtyard.

The palace had become fragile, and restoration began over a decade ago, including US Ambassadors Fund support in 2018. It later became a flagship site of the national 'Dine for Generations' programme. A February 2026 report said the restored palace would open soon, with interpretation spaces and a future museum.

The Jimma Museum in town holds royal items, such as the king's throne and robes.
highlights: Restored wooden palace of Abba Jifar II at Jiren
Gateway to Kafa and Bonga coffee forests
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (roughly October to May); the southwest is very wet in the main rains.
gettingThere: Jimma has an airport (Aba Jifar/Aba Segud, IATA: JIM) with domestic flights from Addis Ababa. By road it is several hours southwest of Addis Ababa (distance not confirmed). The palace is a short taxi or minibus ride from the centre.
tips: Check whether the palace has reopened after restoration before visiting
If the palace is closed or empty, see the royal items in the Jimma Museum
Use Jimma as a base for Bonga and the Kafa forests

name: Kafa Biosphere Reserve and Bonga Coffee Forests
summary: A UNESCO biosphere reserve around Bonga in the Kafa Zone, described as the centre of origin of wild Arabica coffee, with montane forests, wildlife and coffee village visits.
details:
The Kafa Biosphere Reserve was designated by UNESCO in 2010 and lies about 460 km southwest of Addis Ababa. The Kafa Zone is described as the centre of origin and genetic diversity of wild Coffea arabica, and the area holds more than half of Ethiopia's remaining montane forests.

The reserve has a rich mix of wildlife, with hundreds of mammal and bird species reported, including many bats and rare rodents; lions are present but very hard to see. Bonga is the main town and gateway, and the Bonga forest forms part of the reserve.

Visitors come to walk in wild coffee forest, meet coffee farmers and learn about the history of coffee. Tour itineraries often include a day trek to Mankira, a forest locally said to be where Arabica coffee was first discovered.
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season (roughly November to February); this is one of Ethiopia's wettest areas, and trails become very muddy in the rains.
gettingThere: Bonga is about 460 km southwest of Addis Ababa; most travellers fly to Jimma and continue by road (distance not confirmed).
tips: Hire a local guide for forest walks and Mankira
Bring rain gear and waterproof shoes at any time of year
Check whether the Bonga coffee museum is open — reports differ

name: Gambella National Park
summary: Ethiopia's largest lowland wildlife area near the South Sudan border, known for white-eared kob and a huge seasonal antelope migration — but currently under travel warnings.
details:
Gambella National Park was established in 1974 in the far west of Ethiopia, several hundred kilometres from Addis Ababa. Sources give its area as roughly 4,500 to 5,000 square kilometres. The Baro and Akobo rivers flow through the region.

The park has one of Ethiopia's highest concentrations of wildlife, with 69 mammal species recorded. Its flagship species is the white-eared kob. Each year, kob, tiang and Bohor reedbuck move between South Sudan's Boma and Bandingilo national parks and Gambella, a migration described as one of the largest in the world. Nile lechwe are also present.

The park has not been well managed for much of its history. Farming, poaching and refugee camps have reduced wildlife, though anti-poaching work was reported to have doubled animal numbers between 2008 and 2012. Tourist infrastructure is very limited.
bestTimeToVisit: The dry season (roughly November to March) is usually the only time tracks are passable; seek expert local advice.
gettingThere: Gambella town has an airport with domestic flights from Addis Ababa. The park lies to the southwest of the town; access is by 4x4 only, with an experienced operator.
tips: Do not travel without checking current government advice — see notes
Only visit with a reputable operator who has recent experience of the area
Facilities are minimal; bring all supplies
